note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Map and question the scholarly discourse around a topic

evidence.title: Discourse map tagged with Barnett's domains of critical being
evidence.example: You build a one-page map of the scholarly debate on a topic, grouping authors by the position they take and adding one question to each group. Using Barnett's (1997) idea of critical being across knowledge, self and world, you tag each question as aimed at the claim itself, at who it affects, or at what you had assumed. This shows you can map a discourse and question it, not just list sources (for example, three positions on screen time and early language development in education studies).
evidence.artefact: An annotated one-page discourse map with author groups, a question on each group and a short key explaining the Barnett tags.

evidence.title: Source and stakeholder map for a food bank coordinator
evidence.example: You volunteer with a local food bank and the coordinator wants to know what is being said about food insecurity among students. You map the main voices, such as university reports, a charity briefing and two research articles, note where they agree and disagree, and write down the questions they leave open. This shows you can find who is saying what and question it before anyone acts (for example, asking whether the published figures include part-time and commuting students).
evidence.artefact: A two-page briefing note with a map of sources and positions, signed off by the volunteer coordinator.
grounding: professional: Scans a field, market or policy area to find its key players, positions and open questions before acting.
professional: ESCO thinking skills: acquiring and managing information

capabilities.statement: Apply critical thought to the choices made when searching, reading and planning

evidence.title: Search and reading decision log tagged with Delphi dispositions
evidence.example: While preparing a first-year essay, you keep a log of each choice you make: the search terms, the filters, which sources you read and in what order. Beside each choice you note which disposition from Facione's (1990) Delphi report it reflects, such as open-mindedness or diligence in seeking relevant information. This shows critical thought at work before any writing starts (for example, in sport science, choosing to read a study that challenges the textbook view on static stretching).
evidence.artefact: A search and reading decision log of about ten entries, each tagged with a Delphi disposition and a one-line reason.

evidence.title: Planning sheet questioning a manager's brief at a café
evidence.example: In a part-time café job, your manager asks you to find out whether switching to compostable cups is worth it. Before collecting anything, you write down the scope of the question, the sources you will trust, such as council guidance and an independent review, and the assumptions you notice in the brief. This shows you apply critical thought to searching and planning from the start (for example, noting that the most persuasive figures come from the cup supplier itself).
evidence.artefact: A one-page planning sheet listing scope, chosen sources and flagged assumptions, with your manager's written comment on it.
grounding: professional: Questions the sources, scope and assumptions of a piece of work from the start, not only at review.

capabilities.statement: Treat being critical as a habit of mind, not a switch for assessment

evidence.title: Weekly reflections on everyday questioning using Gibbs' Reflective Cycle
evidence.example: Over four weeks you write short reflections, using Gibbs' (1988) Reflective Cycle, on moments when you questioned something outside assessment: a news story, a claim in a lecture, a statistic in a group chat. The analysis and conclusion stages show you asking why you questioned it and what you would do next time. This shows being critical becoming a habit, not something saved for marked work (for example, a psychology student questioning a viral post about learning styles).
evidence.artefact: Four dated reflective log entries following the six stages of Gibbs' cycle, with a closing paragraph on what has changed.

evidence.title: Questions raised as a student society committee member
evidence.example: As a society committee member, you start questioning the society's own habits: claims in recruitment posts, figures in the treasurer's report, assumptions behind event plans. You raise these questions at ordinary meetings where nothing is being assessed, and you check claims before they are acted on. This shows criticality as a habit of mind in everyday settings (for example, asking where the claim that most members prefer evening events came from, then running a quick poll).
evidence.artefact: Meeting minutes showing the questions you raised, the poll results and a short note on the decisions that changed.

capabilities.statement: Recognise the critical thinking skills of analysis and evaluation

evidence.title: Past questions classified by revised Bloom's taxonomy
evidence.example: You collect eight past essay and exam questions from your programme and classify each by the process it demands in Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised Bloom's taxonomy, separating analyse (break down, compare, organise) from evaluate (check, critique, judge). You justify each classification from the steer words and flag questions that need both. This shows you can recognise analysis and evaluation when a task asks for them (for example, in law, 'analyse the reasoning in Donoghue v Stevenson' against 'to what extent was the decision justified').
evidence.artefact: A table of eight questions showing the steer word, the Bloom process, your justification and a tutor's comment on two borderline cases.

evidence.title: Annotated placement requests sorted into analysis or judgement
evidence.example: On an engineering placement you receive three requests from your supervisor. Before starting, you note for each whether it asks for analysis (how a system works and why it fails), a judgement between options, or both, and you confirm your reading with your supervisor. This shows you recognise analysis and evaluation when the brief does not use academic steer words (for example, 'can you look into the pump' turning out to mean 'recommend which replacement to buy').
evidence.artefact: Your annotated copies of the three requests and a short email exchange confirming what each one asked for.
grounding: professional: Recognises when a brief asks for analysis, for a judgement between options, or for both.
professional: Revised Bloom's taxonomy: Analyse, Evaluate

capabilities.statement: Analyse and evaluate a scholarly interpretation

evidence.title: Critique of a historian's interpretation using Delphi core skills
evidence.example: You take one scholarly interpretation and work through it with three core skills from Facione's (1990) Delphi report: analysis, to identify its claims and evidence; evaluation, to judge the strength of its reasoning; and inference, to say what follows and what the author leaves out. You then reach your own view on how far it holds. This shows you can weigh an interpretation, not just summarise it (for example, a historian's argument that the 1834 Poor Law was driven chiefly by cost).
evidence.artefact: A two-page critique sheet mapping the interpretation's argument, your judgement of its strengths and weaknesses, and your inference, with sources cited.

evidence.title: Memo weighing a vendor's wellbeing report against alternatives
evidence.example: On a placement with a school's pastoral team, you are given a supplier's report claiming its wellbeing app reduces pupil anxiety. You analyse its claims, sample and method, then weigh it against two other options the school is considering, and say which is best supported. This shows you can analyse and evaluate an argument made by someone else for a real decision (for example, noting that the report's only study was funded by the supplier and had no comparison group).
evidence.artefact: A one-page memo comparing the report with two alternatives, with your placement supervisor's written feedback.
grounding: professional: Analyses an argument, report or proposal and weighs it against the alternatives.

capabilities.statement: Read a journal article strategically by its structure and method

evidence.title: Reading route record for three articles, method first
evidence.example: You read three journal articles by their structure: abstract and conclusion first, then the method, then the results, and only then the introduction if you need it. For each method section you apply the Delphi skills of interpretation and evaluation (Facione 1990) to decide how far the findings can be trusted. This shows you choose how to read rather than reading front to back (for example, in nursing, checking whether a falls-prevention trial randomised wards or individual patients).
evidence.artefact: A reading record for three articles showing the order you read sections, a method summary and a verdict on how far you rely on each.

evidence.title: Method check of a published study during a software internship
evidence.example: During a summer internship in a software team, you are asked whether a published study supports adopting a new testing tool. You go straight to the method and results, check how the tool was tested and on what kind of code, and only then read the discussion. You brief the team on whether the method justifies the claim (for example, noting that the study used small open-source projects quite unlike your team's large, older system).
evidence.artefact: Your annotated copy of the study with method notes, plus the short written summary or slide you gave the team.
grounding: professional: Reads research and technical reports selectively and checks their method before relying on their findings.

capabilities.statement: Form and justify judgements on the relative importance of factors

evidence.title: Ranked factor judgement built on explicit evaluation criteria
evidence.example: You rank the factors that explain an outcome and justify the order against criteria you state in advance, such as strength of evidence, size of effect and scope. In Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) terms you work at the level of evaluate, checking and critiquing each factor against those criteria rather than listing them. You also say what evidence would change your ranking (for example, in geography, ranking rainfall, land use and drainage as causes of repeated flooding in one town).
evidence.artefact: A ranked factor table with criteria and weightings, a 300-word justification and a note on what evidence would change the ranking.

evidence.title: Live brief recommendation on which factor to tackle first
evidence.example: On a live brief for a small business, you investigate why repeat customers have fallen, weigh the possible causes, and recommend which one the owner should tackle first, stating why and what you set aside. This shows you can form and justify a judgement someone will act on (for example, for an independent bike shop, judging from complaints and sales data that slow repair turnaround matters more than price).
evidence.artefact: A recommendation report with ranked factors and reasons, and the client's written response on the decision they took.
grounding: professional: Recommends one option over others and states why, so that a decision can be taken on it.

capabilities.statement: Write critically, synthesising sources in the discipline's vocabulary

evidence.title: Essay section redrafted from summary into synthesis
evidence.example: You redraft one section of an essay from source-by-source summary into synthesis, grouping sources by the point they make and using the field's own terms. You annotate the redraft to show where it moves from evaluate to create in Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised taxonomy, putting sources together into a new structure that carries your own position (for example, in design, combining usability and inclusive design studies into an argument about hospital wayfinding signs).
evidence.artefact: Before and after versions of one essay section, annotated to show the synthesis moves, the discipline terms used and your own position.

evidence.title: Policy briefing synthesising evidence for a council team
evidence.example: On a placement with a council's public health team, you write a briefing for councillors that draws together research, local data and national guidance. You lead with your conclusion, organise the evidence by theme rather than by source, and use the terms the team works with. This shows you can write critically for readers who must act (for example, framing a briefing on hot food takeaways near schools in terms of health inequalities and upstream interventions).
evidence.artefact: A two-page policy briefing with an evidence synthesis table and your supervisor's sign-off on its accuracy.
grounding: professional: Writes a recommendation that draws the evidence together and reaches a justified conclusion in the field's own terms.

capabilities.statement: Write with authority, aware of how own stance shapes the argument

evidence.title: Stance analysis and positionality commentary on a dissertation chapter
evidence.example: You analyse a draft dissertation chapter using Hyland's (2005) model of stance, marking hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention. You revise so your stance is visible and deliberate, then write a commentary on how your own position shaped which arguments you made strongest. This shows authority that comes from knowing your stance, not hiding it (for example, a teacher researching behaviour policy noticing they boosted claims that matched their own classroom experience).
evidence.artefact: A colour-coded chapter extract showing stance markers before and after revision, with a 500-word positionality commentary.
grounding: model: Stance and engagement model of academic interaction (Hyland 2005)

evidence.title: Insider research report stating the author's position
evidence.example: In a work-based master's project, you research a practice in your own organisation and write a report for senior leaders. You state your stance as an insider at the start, show where it may have shaped your reading of the evidence, and still make a clear case with authority. This shows you can write as an expert while being open about your position (for example, a charity fundraising manager reviewing the donor strategy they helped design).
evidence.artefact: The final report with its positionality section, plus written feedback from a senior leader or academic supervisor.
grounding: practice: work-based master's project in own organisation
